newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OECD sees Swiss economy recovering in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees Swiss economy recovering in 1997/98.

text.p: The Swiss economy is likely to recover in 1997 and 1998 after six years of stagnation, but renewed Swiss franc appreciation caused by concern about the single currency could impede recovery, the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) said.
Switzerland's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) should grow by 0.8 percent in 1997 and 1.8 percent in 1998 after a 0.7 percent 1996 decline in real GDP, the OECD said in a regular annual review.

"With most of the strong exchange rate appreciation during the 1993-95 period now reversed and the European economy gathering strength, the Swiss economy is projected to recover gradually this year and next. Inflation is likely to remain low, given the persisting large output and employment gaps," the report said.
The Swiss year-on-year inflation rate stood at 0.6 percent in May.
However, persistent excess supply of buildings, construction investment is likely to remain a drag on domestic demand in 1997, the report added.
It also said household consumption will again be limited by stagnant real disposable incomes this year, and this will keep the recovery rather modest.

The OECD report also said that as the result of an aggressive policy of monetary easing adopted by the Swiss National Bank (SNB) in mid-1996, combined with the strength of the U.S. dollar, the real effective Swiss franc exchange rate depreciated by some three percent in 1996.
The three-month Euro-Swiss franc interest rate fell to two percent in late 1996 and to 1.7 percent in the first quarter of 1997, reversing its temporary rise to 2.5 percent in mid-1996.

The report also said its projections assume that the SNB keeps short-term interest rates broadly at the current low level in 1997, but tightens a little later on, broadly in line with the assumed policy of Germany's Bundesbank.

This implies an unchanged yield curve and may keep the long-term bond rate discount to German bonds steady at close to two percentage points, it added. -- Greg Calhoun, Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
